candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And Jacob went on his journey to the land of the east, to Laban the brother of Rebecca, and he was with him, and served him for Rachel his daughter one week' — Jubilees specifies one week as the initial service period, with the 'seven years' of Gen 29:20 elsewhere preserved as fourteen years for both wives (Jub 28:9-10). The Tewahedo monastic-novitiate pattern (the novice serves a senior monk for a probationary period before formal acceptance) finds canonical-typological anchor in Jacob's service-for-marriage: bodily-and-laborious commitment proves intention before covenant-relationship is consummated. The Tewahedo discernment-pattern (long service before commitment) is canonically rooted here.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And Laban said unto Jacob: it is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the elder: do this seven days' celebration, and we will give thee her also for the service which thou shalt serve me other seven years' — Laban substitutes Leah for Rachel. Jubilees preserves Laban's deception. Tewahedo Andǝmta exegesis notes the canonical irony: Jacob who deceived his older-brother Esau is now deceived by his uncle Laban who insists on elder-first priority. The Tewahedo Christian moral-formation tradition draws on this episode: divine providence often arranges that the deceiver-from-position-of-weakness becomes the deceived-from-position-of-need — not as retributive punishment but as character-forming pedagogy. Jacob's later integrity is forged through Laban's deception.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And the Lord opened the womb of Leah, and she conceived and bore unto Jacob a son, and he called his name Reuben' — Leah conceives first as the unloved-wife consolation. Jubilees follows Gen 29:32 in attributing the womb-opening to the Lord's compassion on the un-favored. Tewahedo Marian-and-matriarchal piety draws on this canonical pattern: God preferentially attends to the un-favored matriarchs in the patriarchal narratives (Leah, Hagar, the various un-favored wives). The Tewahedo pastoral attention to widowed-or-childless women — extending special intercessory prayer for them — finds canonical anchor in this divine-preference pattern.
